analysis.one_liner: Makes foreign oil cartels like OPEC subject to US antitrust lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee with a favorable report in May 2007 and sat on the Senate calendar for over a year and a half, but it never received a Senate floor vote before the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: OPEC and other foreign governments coordinate oil production and prices today in ways that would be illegal price-fixing if American companies did it, but they are shielded from US courts by sovereign immunity. This bill would strip that shield, declare oil cartels a violation of the Sherman Antitrust Act, and let the US Attorney General sue foreign states that collude to restrict oil supply or inflate prices affecting the US market. It cleared committee but never came up for a vote in the Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: American drivers and businesses that buy gasoline, heating oil, and other petroleum products, who bear the cost of coordinated production cuts by oil-exporting countries. The bill would give the Justice Department a legal tool to challenge that conduct in court.

how_it_helps.text: Declares it illegal under the Sherman Act for any foreign state to act in combination with other states to limit petroleum production, set petroleum prices, or restrain trade when the conduct affects the US market [S2][S3].
Strips sovereign immunity, so a foreign state engaged in oil-cartel conduct could be sued and have judgments enforced in US courts [S2][S3].
Blocks US courts from using the act-of-state doctrine to avoid deciding these cases on the merits, and authorizes the Attorney General to bring enforcement actions [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Foreign oil-producing states and their national oil companies, which could face antitrust suits and damage awards in US courts. The petroleum industry could also be exposed if it is named as a co-conspirator alongside foreign states, and the US government would bear the diplomatic fallout of suing other countries.

drawbacks.text: Suing sovereign oil states in US courts could trigger retaliation: foreign governments could cut oil exports to the US, cut off cooperation on other issues, or treat American firms abroad the way the US treats their state oil companies, which is why US administrations of both parties have historically opposed NOPEC-style legislation [S3] (the bill exposes foreign states to jurisdiction; the retaliation risk is the standard objection to that mechanism).
Enforcement depends entirely on the Attorney General's willingness to sue foreign governments, so the bill creates a tool that a future administration could simply never use [S3].
An antitrust remedy against a production cartel is slow and uncertain; a court judgment cannot quickly lower prices at the pump if a retaliatory supply cut raises them first [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets the single largest external force on American gasoline prices and extends a consumer-protection tool, antitrust law, to foreign cartels that are currently untouchable. The trade-off is real: it risks oil-supply retaliation and diplomatic friction, and it relies on the Justice Department's willingness to use it. Still, it is a genuine, if indirect, attempt to lower energy costs for ordinary consumers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee and was placed on the Senate's calendar of business in May 2007, but Senate leadership never brought it up for a floor vote, and it died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Introduced March 14, 2007 by Senator Kohl with thirteen original cosponsors spanning both parties, and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee [S1][S3][S5].
The Judiciary Committee ordered it reported favorably on April 25, 2007, and it was reported without amendment on May 22, 2007, with Senate Report 110-68 [S5].
It was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 160) on May 22, 2007 — the queue of bills awaiting floor action [S5].
The committee held hearings on May 21, 2008, but no floor vote ever occurred [S5].
The bill never received a Senate floor vote before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: OPEC and other foreign oil-producing states stayed beyond the reach of US antitrust law, and no administration had to manage the diplomatic and oil-supply risks of suing them. American consumers gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Foreign oil cartels, still immune from suit

sides.party_line_note: Support was strongly bipartisan: the bill had 15 cosponsors split 9 Democrats, 4 Republicans, 1 Independent, and 1 Independent Democrat, and its original cosponsors included the Democratic committee chair and four senior Republicans.

industries.note: These states coordinate production cuts and price-setting that raise what Americans pay for gasoline and heating oil, and they currently do so immune from US courts. The bill would strip their sovereign immunity and expose them to antitrust suits and damages.

industries.industry: Petroleum industry (US and international oil companies)
industries.note: Oil majors could benefit if OPEC output rose and prices fell, but they could also be sued as co-conspirators alongside foreign states and could face retaliation against their overseas operations. Their interest in this bill pulled in opposite directions.
Drivers, truckers, and businesses buying fuel stand to gain if cartel conduct restricting supply becomes legally challengeable, since coordinated supply cuts are a direct driver of pump prices.
